summary: Defines MIB objects to configure and monitor MPLS Layer 3 virtual private networks on a label switching router that supports the feature. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: A control panel for setting up and checking private network service on a router.

subtitle: The SNMP management objects for configuring and monitoring BGP/MPLS Layer 3 VPNs on a router.

tldr.problem: Operators who run MPLS Layer 3 VPNs need a standard way to configure and monitor them on each label switching router, instead of vendor-specific tools.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4382 defines the MPLS-L3VPN-STD-MIB module, a set of SNMP tables and scalars covering VRFs, VPN-enabled interfaces, route targets, routes, performance counters and notifications.
tldr.outcome: Any SNMP management system can read and set VPN state on a conforming router. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Max OID sub-identifiers in route table

today: RFC 4382 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2006, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 4382 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Layer 3 Virtual Private Networks (L3VPNs). It describes managed objects to configure and monitor these VPNs on an MPLS Label Switching Router (LSR) that supports the feature.

The document does not re-describe how the VPNs work. It adopts the definitions and mechanisms of RFC 4364 and uses terminology from the MPLS architecture in RFC 3031. Throughout, the terms Provider Edge (PE) and Customer Edge (CE) are folded into just "PE", except where a device is a CE in the carrier's carrier model.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the instruction sheet for a control panel. It does not explain how private networks work; it only lists the switches and meters for them.

sections.title: Management Framework and Prerequisites
sections.content:
MIB objects are normally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and are defined with the Structure of Management Information (SMI). This module is written in SMIv2, which is described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. For the wider management framework the RFC points to RFC 3410.

The tables only make sense if some things are already running. MPLS in general must be configured and operational. Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) paths or traffic-engineered tunnels should be configured between PEs and CEs. The example in the RFC also assumes OSPF or IS-IS is configured and that BGP sessions exist between PEs.
sections.plainLanguage: The control panel only works if the machine behind it is already plugged in and switched on. The roads between the routers must exist first.

sections.title: The Tables and What They Hold
sections.content:
The module is rooted at { mplsStdMIB 11 } and groups its objects into scalars, configuration, performance and route sections. The RFC briefly describes the main tables:

  • mplsL3VpnVrfTable lists the L3VPNs configured on the router. A VRF (Virtual Routing and Forwarding instance) is one device's piece of a VPN. The whole VPN is the collection of VRFs, and that is typically only known in full at the management system, since each device knows just its local VRFs.
  • mplsL3VpnIfConfTable lists the VPN-enabled interfaces tied to a VRF. Each entry corresponds to an Interfaces MIB entry (RFC 2863), so traffic counters live there rather than here.
  • mplsL3VpnVrfPerfTable holds performance objects and augments the VRF table. High-capacity counters are provided for values that may wrap quickly.
  • mplsL3VpnVrfRouteTable holds objects to configure and monitor routes used by a VRF, including a cross-connect pointer into the MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB.
  • The route target table holds the route targets of a VRF.

There is also a security table with a counter of illegally received labels, and a set of scalar objects such as the number of configured VRFs, active VRFs and connected interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one list of private networks, one list of which plugs belong to which network, one list of meters, and one list of routes. Each list answers a different question.

sections.title: VRF Settings and Route Targets
sections.content:
Each VRF entry has a name, an optional VPN ID (as in RFC 2685), a description, a route distinguisher, a creation time, an operational status of up(1) or down(2), interface counts, and route thresholds. A VRF is up when at least one associated interface has ifOperStatus up(1); it is down when there is no such interface or no interface at all. The RFC strongly recommends that all sites supporting VRFs of the same VPN use the same naming convention and the same VPN ID.

Route targets are kept per VRF with a type of import(1), export(2) or both(3). Each VPN-enabled interface also records a classification (carrierOfCarrier, enterprise or interProvider, default enterprise) and the route distribution protocols on the PE-CE link, as a bitmask. The RFC notes that static and OSPF together is a typical configuration.

Rows are created and removed with the standard RowStatus object. Once a row is active, most of its objects cannot be changed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each private network gets a name tag, a secret handshake code, and rules about which messages to take in and send out. You can write these on the panel, but not change them while the network is running.

sections.title: Route Limits and Notifications
sections.content:
A VRF can have a middle threshold, a high threshold and a maximum number of routes. The module defines six notifications, controlled by the read-write mplsL3VpnNotificationEnable object, whose default is false:

  • mplsL3VpnVrfUp and mplsL3VpnVrfDown report changes in the VRF's interface state.
  • mplsL3VpnVrfRouteMidThreshExceeded fires once when the route count passes the middle threshold, and not again until it falls back below it.
  • mplsL3VpnVrfNumVrfRouteMaxThreshExceeded fires when the count exceeds, or tries to exceed, the maximum. A time interval object controls how often it may be reissued; a value of 0 means a single notification, which is the recommended default.
  • mplsL3VpnNumVrfRouteMaxThreshCleared tells the operator the condition has cleared without needing to poll.
  • mplsL3VpnNumVrfSecIllglLblThrshExcd fires when the count of illegally received labels exceeds a configured threshold.

The route table is indexed by many fields. Implementers must keep the object identifiers of its column instances to no more than 128 sub-identifiers, or the objects cannot be accessed with SNMPv1, SNMPv2c or SNMPv3.
sections.plainLanguage: The router can ring a bell when a private network gets too full of routes, when it goes up or down, or when it receives something it should not. You can turn the bells on or off.

sections.title: A Worked Setup
sections.content: Section 6 gives a short example of defining a VRF, a route target and a route distinguisher, assuming MPLS (via LDP or RSVP-TE), an IGP, and BGP sessions between PEs are already in place. It creates a VRF named RED with description "Intranet of Company ABC" and route distinguisher 100:1 using createAndGo(4), then creates import and export route target rows. The RFC says it is meant to be read after the MIB itself and does not illustrate every nuance.
sections.plainLanguage: The example is like filling in a form for a new private network called RED, giving it a code number, and saying what it should share with others.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns that anything that can be configured can be misconfigured, with potentially disastrous results. The read-write and read-create objects, especially those in the VRF, interface and route tables, could disrupt network traffic if reached without authorization, notably for VRFs already in use.

Some readable objects are also sensitive, since they reveal VRF interfaces, configuration and links to other MPLS settings. The RFC says SNMPv3 VACM and USM MUST be used with any v3 agent that implements this module, recommends SNMPv3 cryptographic security, and says deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who gets hold of the control panel could mess up everyone's private networks. So only trusted people with a proper lock should be allowed to touch it.

sections.title: IANA Assignment
sections.content: MPLS-related standards-track MIB modules are rooted under the mplsStdMIB subtree from RFC 3811. IANA assigned { mplsStdMIB 11 } to the MPLS-L3VPN-STD-MIB module defined here. New assignments in that subtree can only be made via a Standards Action.
sections.plainLanguage: The module got its own official shelf number in the big library of management modules, so nobody else uses the same one.
